newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish group tries to ease Catholic parade fears.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish group tries to ease Catholic parade fears.

text.p: Northern Ireland's powerful Protestant Orange Order tried on Wednesday to ease anxiety about a contentious parade by asking for tolerance from Roman Catholic homeowners in the area.

The group, whose thousands of members hold province-wide pro-British parades each summer, announced it had sent an open letter to 1,500 Catholic homes in a "sincere and genuine attempt" to defuse tension about a march near their homes next month.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, eager for resolution of a controversy that is hampering efforts for an all-round peaceful settlement in the province, welcomed the initiative as a positive bid "to promote understanding".
However, Catholic residents in the town of Portadown gave it a lukewarm welcome and called for talks on the march.

The Orange Order rejects Catholic charges that parades are nakedly anti-Irish. It says the Order's march next month is being held to commemorate the province's Protestants and Catholics who died during World War One, and as a display of traditional allegiance to the Protestant religion.

"We see our parade as an outward witness to our sincere belief in the (Protestant) Reformed Faith. For that reason, we see attacks on our parades as both a denial of civil liberties and an attack on our religion."

Last July the British-ruled province was plunged into turmoil when police banned "Orangemen" from parading through Portadown's Irish nationalist Garvaghy Road but then reversed the decision when confronted with angry Protestant protests.
Two Catholics died during the incident. Protestant and Catholic rioters attacked police in several towns for many days.
A policeman was kicked to death by a mob in the town of Ballymony on Sunday. Media linked the murder to Protestant fury over a march being prohibited in another Catholic village.
Resentment about march bans has simmered for a year, souring a political climate already destabilised by rival Irish republican and pro-British Loyalist guerrilla violence.

Multi-party talks on the political future of the province restarted on Tuesday after a break for the British election campaign. Sinn Fein, the political wing of the banned IRA, remains outside the talks because of the IRA's refusal to reinstate a ceasefire in its bloody campaign to oust British forces from the province.

In its letter the Orange Order said that it had curtailed the Portadown march in recent years to accommodate nationalist objections. It was a small parade with hymns played by accordion bands, the letter said.
